newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - Billy Strayhorn, a quiet genius, wins a stage at last.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Billy Strayhorn, a quiet genius, wins a stage at last.

text.p: Listen to the music of Duke Ellington and invariably you hear someone else, a little known composer and arranger who worked with Ellington for three decades but who only recently has begun to win recognition as his equal.

The man was Billy Strayhorn, composer of such enduring classics such as "Lush Life," "Chelsea Bridge," and "Take the A Train," signature tune of the Ellington orchestra. Perhaps even more significantly, he wrote in close collaboration with Ellington, swapping ideas, creating arrangements, fleshing out harmonies and lyrics on tunes like "Satin Doll," which was only a riff before Strayhorn brought it to life.

Few people outside the close-knit world of jazz musicians knew of Strayhorn's crucial role in the Ellington organisation. While Ellington gave him credit -- and they considered each other best friends -- it was never at his own expense. Ellington's name after all sold the concert tickets.

Strayhorn remained in Ellington's shadow his entire life, dying of cancer in 1967 at age 51, a genius without a public following. Now that may be changing. With recent critically acclaimed biography "Lush Life" (Farrar, Straus and Giroux) by David Hajdu, and several recordings focusing on Strayhorn's work, the shadow is finally lifting.

"He was a genuinely heroic figure because he defied so many of the rules -- the things our culture values so strongly like the pursuit of fame, fortune and ego gratification," Hajdu told Reuters. He suggests that another reason for Strayhorn's relative anonymity was that he was gay -- and openly so in an intolerant era. He could afford to be out of the closet in the 1950s within the security of the Ellington fold, but had he been on his own as a gay, black bandleader he would have been the target of prejudice.

As a result, only his close friends and the musicians who played his works really knew of his artistic accomplishments -- ones which are now being viewed as on a par with Ellington and other great composers of 20th century American music.

"There wasn't anybody who didn't want to talk to me about Strayhorn," said Hajdu, who worked on the book for a dozen years and interviewed scores of people. "As soon as I raised his name in the jazz world everybody had something to say. It was like a dam waiting to break open. People wanted to talk about him but no one had ever been asked before."

Lena Horne, who called Strayhorn the only man she ever loved, invited Hajdu to her house for an interview. He said dozens of others who have since died filled in the blanks of Strayhorn's extraordinary story.

Along with the book, an artistic portrait of Strayhorn is emerging from previously unknown compositions stored in the Ellington archive at the Smithsonian Institution in Washington. Walter van de Leur, a Dutch musicologist who discovered the works, found that many had never been performed and few outside of Ellington's small circle even knew they existed. Van de Leur said Strayhorn on average composed at least a piece a week for the 30 years he worked with the Duke.

Eight of the newly discovered works, which seem out of character with the Ellington Orchestra, appear on a recent CD from Kokopelli called "Portrait of a Silk Thread," played by the Dutch Jazz Orchestra. Nonesuch this year also issued a recording of Strayhorn material played by pianist Fred Hersch, "Passion Flower."

Dovetailing with the Hajdu book, Verve compiled a disk of Strayhorn works by the likes of Ella Fitzgerald, Ben Webster, Joe Henderson, Sarah Vaughan and Oscar Peterson, among others. And Blue Note is reissuing the only solo work ever recorded by Strayhorn, out of print for decades.

On these recordings, you hear the personality of the composer unfold. Strayhorn's ballads hint at sadness and longing but the melodies are infectious. The tunes swing hard at times but always come across with an airy lightness.

He personified the big band era but added an element that was more complex, probing and introspective. He brought in elements of western classical music and was not afraid to go beyond swing, to early forms of modal jazz in the 1940s that would not be explored for several years.

His best compositions, like "Lush Life" or "Something to Live For," express an after-hours melancholy. He called this time, when the martinis from the night before are still flowing, "halfway to dawn" and it was his favourite -- a time of vulnerability and honesty.
"Who is Billy Strayhorn? At first it was a mystery to me but listening to his music I couldn't help being struck by the depth and beauty and majesty of it," Hajdu said. "How could no one know him?"
